data.title: Best Stocks Under $10 to Buy Now
data.description:
Before I get into the best stocks under $10 to buy right now, let me start with this disclaimer: share price doesn’t really matter.

As Warren Buffett is fond of saying, “Price is what you pay, value is what you get.” That’s true. Still, for someone starting a portfolio with just a couple thousand dollars, investing in 50 shares of a $10 stock seems way more appealing than investing in one share of a $1,000 stock.

If you want to diversify, you don’t want to devote half your portfolio to one share of Amazon (AMZN) or Alphabet (GOOG). You can create a portfolio of 10 stocks even if you only have $2,000 or $3,000 to invest.

To do it, however, you need to find low-priced stocks.

[text_ad]

From there, it depends on what you’re looking for in your investments: long-term gains or a quick return in a prime turnaround stock candidate.

If you want to find the best stocks under $10 that you can buy and hold for a while, you should start with stocks that have already been trending upward for some time. A strong chart, after all, is one of the best indicators of future gains. For that, I screened for stocks with share prices under $10 that are trading above their 50-day moving average. There were quite a few on the list, which was a bit of a surprise given the weak market of late, so I narrowed it down to companies with a potentially powerful “story” (as my colleague Mike Cintolo would call it) as well.

Best Stocks Under $10: Algonquin Power & Utilities Corp. (AQN)

Algonquin is a Canadian utility company that provides everything from electricity to water to wastewater collection, plus natural gas utility systems and transmission. It serves 1.27 million customers in not only Canada but the U.S., Chile and Bermuda. It has operations in 14 U.S. states. The company is on track for 7.6% revenue growth and 5.9% EPS growth this year with earnings growth accelerating to 13.9% next year (with 4.2% revenue growth). Meanwhile, the stock (a mid-cap) trades at just 14x forward earnings and less than 1x book value, despite a 10% rally since the start of September. Shares trade for just 5.50, and the average one-year price target among analysts is 6.32 – a 15% premium to the current price. A 4.7% dividend yield adds to AQN’s appeal.

Best Stocks Under $10: Coty Inc. (COTY)

Coty sells well-known beauty products in the U.S. and overseas. The company has two divisions: Prestige and Consumer Beauty. Its products include fragrances, cosmetics, skin and body care, etc., manufacturing, marketing and selling brands such as Burberry, Calvin Klein, Hugo Boss, Marc Jacobs, Tiffany and many others. Department stores, drug store and e-retailers are among its more prominent clients.

And while Coty’s sales have slipped in recent years, it has become far more profitable, with earnings on track to expand from 21 cents a share last year to 36 cents a share this year. The stock has risen accordingly, up 40% year to date and more than doubling from less than 2 per share in June to exactly 4 per share now. Of course, COTY used to be a $13 stock as recently as 2024, so it’s really just getting up off the mat. The lack of top-line growth is concerning, but the stock is cheap at just 11x forward earnings and 0.6x sales. Coming off a good quarter (61% earnings growth) and with plenty of momentum in the share price, it’s worth a low-priced flyer.

Best Stocks Under $10: Peloton Interactive (PTON)

Remember during Covid when this company (along with Zoom, Chegg and a few other online-only outfits) was all the rage? That didn’t last, even though plenty of folks (myself included) still own and use Pelotons, the interactive subscription exercise bikes and treadmills. But sales are down 40% from those Covid peaks, declining from a high of $4 billion in 2021 to $2.44 billion in the recently completed 2026 fiscal year. And the stock has been eviscerated, plummeting from a high above 150 a share in late 2020 to just 5 a share now. It seems the selling may have been overdone – the company is profitable for the first time in years, and those profits are expected to more than double in FY ’27 (to 38 cents a share from 14 cents on an adjusted basis last year). A $600 million debt refinancing plan earlier this month gave shares an extra boost – and the company a jolt of much-needed cash. Also, sales actually increased 2% in the latest (fiscal first) quarter – a third consecutive quarter of sales growth, an encouraging sign. Plus, free cash flow more than doubled.

Trading at less than 14x forward earnings and 1x sales, PTON looks like a strong buy-low candidate … with a very low share price.

[author_ad]

*This post has been updated from an original version published in 2024.

data.title: Don’t Miss the Opportunity in Fixed-Rate Investments
data.description:
This market is increasingly volatile and troubling.

The S&P 500 is now down more than 6% from the high and could be headed to correction territory (down 10%). Several issues are shaking things up.

The already struggling technology trade is getting slapped with a controversy at Nvidia (NVDA). At the same time, tensions with Iran are increasing and investors still can’t decide if the Democratic takeover of Congress is good or bad for the market.

But perhaps the most troubling aspect of the current market is interest rates. The benchmark 10-year Treasury rate soared above 5% in September and October to the highest level since 2002. While the rate has since come off the high, it still hovers above 5%, the level at which the market considers problematic.

The Treasury rate is the benchmark used for mortgages, car loans, personal loans, and any kind of longer-term interest rate. Higher loan rates make borrowing less affordable and increase costs for businesses. That’s a big part of the reason 84% of stocks on the S&P 500 fell 10% or more from the high and 60% of stocks fell at least 20% after the Treasury rate moved above 5% earlier this fall.

Interest rates had trended lower for forty years prior to this decade. The benchmark 10-year Treasury rate went from an astronomical 16% in 1981 all the way down to about 0.5% in 2020 during the pandemic. The downward trend was unmistakable, although bouncy at times.

That downward trend ended in 2022. The rate went from 1.5% at the beginning of the year to 4.23% by October. The rate had averaged between 2% and 2.5% over the decade prior. What happened? Inflation happened.

Inflation puts upward pressure on interest rates as fixed-rate investors demand to be compensated. The Consumer Price Index (CPI), by which inflation is usually measured, averaged 1.77% from 2000 through 2019. The inflation rate skyrocketed to over 9% by June of 2022, the highest level in more than 40 years. But inflation has since moderated.

The CPI inflation rate fell to less than 4% by the middle of 2023 and averaged under 3% from late 2024 until early this year. CPI has moved higher and averaged around 3.5% since March because of the inflationary pressures of high oil prices as a result of the war with Iran.

While inflation has come down, interest rates have not. The 10-year Treasury rate had peaked at just about 5% in October of 2023, after which it started trending lower. But the rate has now eclipsed the previous peak.

It is for good reason that rates have moved higher while inflation has come way down since 2022. Virtually no one expected the astronomical inflation rates to last, and they haven’t. Bond rates don’t get priced to compensate investors for 10 years of an inflation rate that is likely to come way down in a matter of months.

But here we are four years later, and the inflation rate is still double the average of what it was in the first two decades of this century. The long-lingering higher inflation does require compensation to fixed-rate investors.

[text_ad]

The high energy prices have lingered for more than eight months now. The increased inflationary pressure prompts the Fed to get aggressive and counter those pressures by raising the fed funds rate. Higher short-term rates also put upward pressure on longer rates.

There are also demand pressures. Higher demand tends to increase prices, and interest rates are the price of money. Technology companies are borrowing hundreds of billions of dollars to fund data centers and other AI infrastructure. That creates competition for fixed rates while the government continues to sell massive amounts of bonds to fund its ungodly amount of debt.

It’s also a strong economy. Third-quarter GDP was 3.4%, the highest growth in years and well above the average growth rate of the past decade. Forecasts for fourth-quarter GDP are also quite bullish. A stronger economy puts upward pressure on interest rates, and demand for borrowing increases.

Of course, the war with Iran will end at some point. That should drive oil prices, and likely interest rates, lower. But for now, interest rates are still near the highest level in two decades. Therein lies the opportunity. The same situation that spells trouble for borrowers also presents opportunity for income investors.

Prudent investors don’t put all their investable assets in stocks, especially older ones in a lower risk class. Earning a good return on your non-stock invested assets will bolster your overall returns and make it easier to stay invested in turbulent stock markets. Plus, these assets can also provide a much-needed income. But it’s been so long since decent returns on safe assets were available that many investors have forgotten about this important aspect of portfolio management.

Fixed-income yields are now near the highest level since the beginning of this century. Quality fixed-income investments are no longer paying a measly 2%. Now, you can get investment-grade-rated bonds and preferred stocks paying 5%, 6% or even 7%. And they have less downside now, with rates near a multi-decade high.

It’s true that interest rates can still move higher from here, and prices of fixed-income securities will fall if they do. But higher interest rates from here will likely put pressure on the market and the economy. That pressure would likely drive interest rates lower. Also consider that fixed-income investments generally have a longer holding period than most stocks. Even if interest rates trend higher in the near term, they are far less likely to average higher than they are today over the next five years or so.

The recent interest rate spike is presenting a golden opportunity to lock in the highest rates in decades and partially fill the fixed-income void for most investors.

[author_ad]

data.title: 3 High-Dividend Stocks with Impressive Growth
data.description:
When investors think about growth stocks, they usually picture fast-growing technology companies that reinvest their profits to expand their businesses.

Contrast that with dividend stocks, the slow-moving investments that provide steady income but relatively little appreciation.

But as we’ve seen this year, that’s not always the case.
High-dividend stocks, as measured by the Vanguard High Dividend Yield ETF (VYM), have significantly outperformed growth stocks this year. VYM’s one-year return of 16.5% is more than double the 7.6% return of the Nasdaq and more than four times greater than the 3.1% return of the Roundhill Magnificent Seven ETF (MAGS).

And when you combine those rising stock prices with years of dividends, the returns can be surprisingly strong.

That’s particularly attractive for investors looking to generate income without giving up the opportunity for capital appreciation.

Consider three stocks from very different industries: Altria Group (MO), Aegon (AEG) and NLI Holdings (NL).

All three currently offer dividend yields above 5%. And all three have produced positive returns over the past year and the past five years.

Let’s take a closer look.

[text_ad]

3 High-Dividend Stocks Boasting Solid Total Returns

1. Altria Group (MO): Big Dividends and Big Returns

Altria is one of the best-known dividend stocks on the market.

The company owns Marlboro, one of the most recognizable cigarette brands in the United States, along with several other tobacco and nicotine products.

Cigarettes aren’t exactly a growth industry. Smoking rates have been declining for decades, and tobacco companies face ongoing regulatory pressure.

But Altria has managed to generate substantial cash flow despite those challenges, largely because of its pricing power and established brands.

And much of that cash goes directly to shareholders.

Altria recently raised its quarterly dividend by 4.7%, to $1.11 per share, or $4.44 annually.

At a recent share price just shy of 79, that works out to a dividend yield of 5.6%.

Even more impressive, Altria has increased its dividend 61 times over the past 57 years.

But investors haven’t just been collecting dividends.

Over the past year, Altria has delivered a total return of 45.3%, including reinvested dividends.

And over the past five years, its total return is 156% (with dividends reinvested).

That’s an exceptional performance for a company operating in an industry with declining demand.

Of course, any investment thesis has to factor in the biggest drag on shares: Cigarette sales volumes continue to decline, and the company’s success thus far has relied on the expansion of its smoke-free products.

Still, Altria’s combination of dependable cash generation, a long dividend history and strong stock performance makes it worth a look for income investors.

2. Aegon (AEG): An Insurance Stock with Strong Long-Term Growth

Aegon is a major Dutch international financial services company (although shareholders approved a plan to redomicile to the U.S. some time next year) with operations in life insurance, retirement products and investment management. Its businesses include Transamerica, a well-known provider of insurance and retirement services in the United States.

The company has been working to simplify its operations, improve profitability and return more money to shareholders.

And those efforts are producing results.

In the first half of 2026, Aegon’s operating earnings rose 9% to €804 million, while operating capital generation increased 27%.

The company also reported a 54% increase in new individual life insurance sales at Transamerica.

Those improvements are helping support a growing dividend.

Aegon raised its interim dividend for 2026 by 11%, to €0.21 per share. Based on its last share price just shy of 8.50, the stock offers a trailing dividend yield of about 5.7%.

And the shares have been strong as well. Over the past year, Aegon has generated a 15.3% total return, including reinvested dividends.

Five-year returns are even stronger, totaling 124% with dividends reinvested.

That’s an impressive longer-term return for a company in a relatively mature industry.

Of course, it’s worth noting that insurance companies are sensitive to changes in interest rates and the performance of their portfolio assets. A significant market downturn could put pressure on earnings.

Still, Aegon’s improving operations, growing dividend and strong five-year returns make it an interesting choice for investors seeking both income and growth.

3. NLI Holdings (NL): A Little-Known Dividend Stock

The third company on our list is probably unfamiliar to most investors.

NLI Holdings (NL), formerly known as NL Industries, is a small, diversified holding company involved in industrial products and chemicals.

Its businesses include a controlling interest in CompX International, which manufactures security products and components for the marine industry.

NLI also owns a significant stake in Kronos Worldwide, a producer of titanium dioxide, a chemical used in paints, plastics and other industrial products.

It’s not an especially glamorous business. But that doesn’t mean you should ignore it.

NLI has benefited from improving results at both CompX and Kronos.

In the third quarter of 2026, the company reported net income of $12.7 million, or $0.26 per share, compared with a loss of $7.8 million, or $0.16 per share, a year earlier.

CompX’s quarterly sales rose 10%, while its segment profit increased from $4.8 million to $6.4 million.

Meanwhile, Kronos reported an 18% increase in quarterly sales, helped by market-share gains and higher selling prices.

The company currently pays a quarterly dividend of $0.10 per share, or $0.40 annually.

With shares recently trading around 7.30, that translates to a dividend yield of 5.6%.

The dividend has increased from $0.07 per quarter in 2023 to $0.10 today. The company also made special dividend payments in 2024 and 2025, so there’s a strong shareholder-friendly bent to the company when business conditions allow.

And the stock has produced respectable returns.

Over the past year, NL has delivered a total return of 36%, including dividend reinvestment.

Over the past five years, its total return with dividends reinvested is 51.6%. So while it hasn’t been quite as strong as the other names on this list, it’s put up solid numbers just the same.

It should be noted, however, that NLI is a relatively small company, with a market capitalization of roughly $350 million. As a result, shares are very thinly traded and require special handling and more time to get into and out of positions.

The company’s earnings also depend heavily on industrial demand and the performance of its subsidiaries, so an economic slowdown would be a major drag on shares.

Nevertheless, NLI offers a combination of high income and improving financial results that could appeal to investors willing to consider smaller stocks.

High Dividends Don’t Have to Mean Low Growth

One of the biggest misconceptions about dividend investing is that investors must choose between income and growth.

But investors who focus only on fast-growing companies that pay little or no dividend may be overlooking some attractive opportunities.

Altria, Aegon and NLI Holdings operate in very different industries, yet all three have rewarded shareholders through a combination of dividend income and stock appreciation.

For investors seeking steady income without giving up the potential for growth, they’re three stocks worth watching.

[author_ad]

data.title: Why Value Stocks Are Beating Growth Stocks for the First Time in a Decade
data.description:
Value stocks are having a banner year.

The Vanguard Morningstar Value ETF (VTV) is up 20% year to date, putting it on track for its best year since 2021 (23.7% return). But it’s not just the performance in value stocks as an asset class that’s been impressive; it’s their outperformance of growth stocks and the broad market that truly stands out.

As of trading last Friday, November 13, the tech- and growth-heavy Nasdaq was up just 9.4% so far this year. The last time the VTV topped the Nasdaq was a decade ago, in 2016, when the 14.1% run-up in value stocks more than doubled the 5.9% return in the Nasdaq that year.

As mega-cap tech names, the Mag. 7 and now artificial intelligence plays have gained in prominence in recent years, value stocks have often been left in the dust. The performance hasn’t been bad, mind you; entering 2026, the average annual return in the VTV in the 2020s was just under 9%, roughly in line with the historic annual return in the S&P 500. But it paled in comparison to the performance in growth stocks, with the Nasdaq up 177% since the beginning of 2020.

[text_ad]

This year, that script has been flipped.

Why Investors are Pivoting to Value Stocks

The AI trade has finally run into some skepticism as investors worry that companies are spending far more than they’re earning, and the general public fears that AI might take their jobs, bring environmentally harmful data centers to their towns or even “kill us all,” as a couple industry whistleblowers warned. Meanwhile, the war in Iran has sent prices – particularly oil prices – back into the stratosphere, forcing the Fed to raise interest rates again. That has put a damper on growth. But with the economy still doing fine and the bull market very much intact, investors haven’t gone away. They’ve simply pivoted to the many undervalued and unloved names that had been left in the dust the last few years as Wall Street drooled over AI.

This year, however, investors have shifted their gaze away from AI, at least since the furious April-May run-up. And what they’ve found are a lot of growing companies in non-AI industries that are trading at relative bargains.

I compare what has happened in 2026 to when my wife and I take our kids’ iPads away for a week. At first, they complain; but then, they find other things to do – play soccer and football outside, play hide-and-seek inside, ride their bikes down to the nearby country store to get Poppis (“healthy,” prebiotic-infused soda for kids) and a cider donut. Usually, they have way more fun once they stop staring at screens and start looking at (and enjoying) everything else around them – a lesson we all (myself included!) could probably learn from in this screen-heavy era.

Value Is Beating Growth … But Another Growth Rally Would Help

It’s not a perfect comparison. After all, the AI boom has delivered some fantastic, wealth-building profits over the last few years. But for those of us who seek value and prioritize having a diverse portfolio, it has not been as fruitful as it was for those investors with nothing but AI and Mag. 7 stocks in their portfolio. Or at least it wasn’t until this year. Now, after a decade of underperformance, value investors are being rewarded. It’s why six stocks in my Cabot Value Investor newsletter portfolio have reached my price target this year, including two in the last month alone.

Hopefully there will be many more winners to come as value stocks continue to outperform. And even if the AI trade isn’t dead, and tech and chip stocks come roaring back … value stocks will probably do just fine, like they did during the aforementioned April and May rally.

Value stocks are a good place to be right now. If you need help finding the right ones, you can join me at Cabot Value Investor by clicking here.

[author_ad]

data.title: Value Investing Opportunities in a Stealth Bear Market
data.description:
This year has witnessed one of the most paradoxical market environments in memory. Although the major indexes, led by the S&P 500, have remained buoyant through much of 2026, below the surface there has been what can only be described as a “stealth” bear market. But through the mixed performance and periodic volatility spikes, the market has also provided value-oriented investors with opportunities, which we’ll discuss here.

A Stealth Bear Market Is Hiding in the S&P 500

But first, consider that while the S&P has spent much of the last couple of months around 2-3% below its all-time high, more than 40% of S&P 500 stocks were at least 20% below their 52-week highs as of earlier this month. Even more tellingly, the average individual stock listed on the NYSE has entered bear market territory, trading roughly 21% below its 2026 peak, even though the headline indexes have masked much of this damage.

What this suggests is that we’re witnessing a classic internal correction in the broad market, with a relatively small group of mega-cap leaders keeping the SPX elevated even as most of its component stocks are underperforming. And the reason for the broader weakness isn’t hard to discover: It’s primarily related to surging longer-dated Treasury yields.

Indeed, the so-called “risk-free” discount rate for the 10-year Treasury isn’t far below the recent highs of 5.3%, its highest level since 2002. And since higher discount rates reduce the present value of future earnings and cash flows, it makes stocks appear less attractive at existing prices.

It’s no surprise, then, that the last several weeks have witnessed a soaring number of NYSE stocks making new 52-week lows, with many days showing new lows in the triple digits while new highs are sometimes merely low-double digits. Many of those new lows are bond funds or interest rate-sensitive equities.

Why AI Stocks Are Under Pressure

But while some rate-sensitive industries are still experiencing selling pressure, formerly strong AI-related names have lately been victims of the stealth bear, and for obvious reasons: Recent fears that the AI trade is “overdone” continue to percolate as of mid-November.

[text_ad]

On that score, remaining under selling pressure as of this writing is one of the market’s core proxies for the AI buildout, Nvidia (NVDA), which fell to a 16-month low on November 12 after the sudden resignation of its CEO. The stock’s recent plunge reminded everyone that the all-things-AI trade remains tenuous after what looked like a possible “wash-out” bottom of the leading AI infrastructure and support stocks earlier this month.

As for why specifically investors are in panic mode over AI stocks, conventional thinking suggests that the market is moving from rewarding AI spending and growth potential to demanding evidence that the enormous investments in AI infrastructure—to the tune of hundreds of billions of dollars—will lead to worthwhile returns. Additional reasons include fears over the data center builders’ increasing reliance on debt financing—with the aforementioned rising interest rate environment contributing to these fears—as well as uncertainties over how quickly AI adoption will be monetized.

But here’s another possible reason: physical AI data center overbuilding. According to statistics from Cleanview, 68% to 75% of all tracked (mainly hyperscale) data centers in the U.S. aren’t yet operational and are either actively under construction or in the planning or announced phases. That’s a substantial development pipeline, and there’s no guarantee that all of this planned capacity will ultimately be needed or prove economically viable.

And while I may be stretching the analogy, I think it’s somewhat comparable to China’s infrastructure and property overbuilding trend of recent years that led to a prolonged property slump in that country.

Thus, it can be argued the market is worried that today’s oversized investments based on projections of future AI demand may not see the predicted returns materialize as quickly—or as strongly—as developers and investors anticipate.

To that end, a July study by McKinsey found that portions of the AI infrastructure ecosystem exhibit “bubble-like characteristics,” particularly among highly leveraged AI infrastructure intermediaries and companies with negative cash flow. And if the aforementioned debt financing and related interest rate concerns persist, this could make future financing more expensive and difficult to attain, thus amplifying the damage from increased worries over the overbuilding aspects of the data center boom.

As a result of these salient factors, I think avoiding the temptation to jump in and buy the beaten-down AI names is ideal right now. Instead, I suggest that tech sector participants wait for the semiconductor indexes and ETFs to confirm a bottom instead of assuming the worst is over for the AI sector.

Where Value Investing Opportunities Are Emerging

That said, even within the current “stealth bearish” environment, the market has provided some attractive opportunities for value-oriented investors. Indeed, many of the turnaround stocks in our Cabot Turnaround Letter portfolio have benefited in recent weeks from the recent rotation towards value stocks in the wake of the AI crash. And that’s because beaten-down value stocks are often among the biggest beneficiaries of broad market weakness, as investors gravitate toward deeply discounted, previously overlooked equities—particularly those with strengthening financial profiles—in anticipation of an eventual market rebound.

And it’s worth noting that most beneficiaries of a confirmed market bottom are typically those stocks and industry groups that did the best job of resisting the selling pressure during the correction period. And right now, many of the stocks fitting that description are in the defensive healthcare and consumer staples sectors.

To that end, these two areas are where I see the most opportunity for turnaround-focused investors going forward and where I suggest participants looking to hedge their tech sector exposure look closely.

[author_ad]

data.title: The Nvidia Mess—and What It Means for the Stock
data.description:
The serious dustup over Nvidia chip exports to China exploded this week with a gripping story involving Nvidia’s founder and (now former) CEO Jensen Huang.

Specifically, a romantic relationship with Alice Huang (no relation), an alleged Chinese spy and CEO of a Singapore-domiciled company that is an Nvidia client. It seems that some advanced Nvidia chips eventually made their way from Singapore to China.

Importantly, the Wall Street Journal reported that as recently as the summer of last year, Singapore was one of Nvidia’s biggest markets, generating 22% of the chip maker’s revenue, up 81% from a year earlier. Then, it abruptly disappeared from the company’s financial disclosures.

This revelation ties together the current U.S. advanced chip export ban to China plus the possibility that classified intelligence regarding either the U.S. government or Nvidia was compromised.

The media is intensively following up on this, and other allegations are possible. Senators Warren and Coons are already in action regarding hearings.

The Nvidia mess could also negatively impact the forthcoming Anthropic (ANT) IPO.

[text_ad]

This story is evolving day by day as Nvidia (NVDA) stock is already down sharply over the last month. The downside risk is significant, and the blast radius in the AI world and Washington will widen considerably if it is confirmed that Jensen Huang shared sensitive or classified information.

Nvidia is at the center of AI – the linchpin of the AI story.

Due to the company’s dominant market position in advanced AI chips, a strong balance sheet, close ties to Washington power players, a high growth rate, and extensive circular vendor and shadow financing, it is also essentially the central bank of AI, something that Bloomberg explored in great detail last year.

It is fine to buy some Nvidia (NVDA) stock on current weakness, but I advise caution as events can take an uncertain turn and the Nvidia board has already taken the step of naming a replacement interim CEO, Colette Kress.

Regarding Alice Huang, more and more is coming out regarding her past operations and connections to a wide variety of Chinese businesses and organizations.

The infographic on this page from The Wire China connects the dots.

Chinese tech firms are now leapfrogging across industries and sectors, moving from smartphones to EVs to robotics. EVs, drones, and robotics share many of the same core components, like batteries, sensors, and electronic controllers. These days, nearly every major Chinese tech firm has its own AI models, custom chips, and robots. You might call them physical AI conglomerates. Xiaomi (XIACY) recently claimed to have its own humanoid robots doing autonomous 8-hour shifts on its EV production line.

The chief benefactor of the Nvidia mess is China, and particularly Huawei. In 1984, Shanghai Bell was the first China telecom equipment joint venture, and other joint telecom ventures with foreign companies soon followed, including Huawei. By the 1990s, China had successfully shifted from importing telecom equipment to producing most of it domestically through these joint ventures.

Huawei now stands at the heart of China’s advances and ambitions. Founded in 1987 as a small supplier of telephone switches, Huawei has transformed into a manufacturing and digital giant with over $100 billion a year in revenue. A partial subsidiary is currently providing undersea cables connecting three continents and semiconductor chips.

It is time for a new, permanent Nvidia CEO to bring in a new, tighter operating system. The stock may rise on such an announcement.

[author_ad]

data.title: Is the AI Trade Over? 1 Defensive Stock to Buy Instead
data.description:
Is the AI trade over?

No one knows for sure, but economist and market strategist Jim Paulsen thinks it could be.

He points out that the relative performance of AI stocks has been leading the increase in the ratio of New Era spending to real GDP since early 2023. It follows that the current underperformance of AI stocks could be warning of a significant decline in New Era spending compared to overall real GDP going forward. After all, stocks typically anticipate economic and sector trends – as was the case during the AI boom time of the past three years.

If he’s right, it makes sense to tilt your portfolio more towards “old era” non-AI stocks. They’ve been vastly outperforming AI stocks in the past month. During that time, his S&P 500 Old Era Stock Price Index (comprising a market cap weighting of the nine S&P 500 sectors excluding the New Era technology & communications sectors) has risen by 4.2%, compared to a 27% decline in the Bank of America AI Beneficiaries Index. This could be the start of a trend that has old-era stocks outperforming AI stocks going forward.

Old-era stocks have a lot of ground to make up. They made up 80% of the S&P 500 ten years ago, compared to just 50% in early October, Paulsen points out in his Paulsen Perspectives on Substack.

A Defensive Dividend Stock to Buy if AI Stocks Keep Falling

PepsiCo (PEP)

If you want to diversify away from AI stocks in favor of old-era and more defensive names, consider owning PepsiCo. Snack foods and fizzy drinks are about as far away from AI as an investor could get.

Shares of the brand powerhouse were recently down around 20% from their early February highs.

In the weakness, a director who knows the snack and soft drink space quite well because of a lifetime of experience in the business and at PepsiCo stepped up to buy $23.7 million worth of stock.

The purchase makes sense because there are good reasons to think that PepsiCo results may improve from here.

Investors doubt a mini turnaround in the works will pan out. Buying shares here is a bet they will be wrong. I think it is a good bet, given the director’s enthusiasm for the stock.

PepsiCo is doing some renovation work in its kitchens, and improvements to the business look like they will boost sales performance from here. That’s clearly what this director is counting on, with his huge purchase.

Third-quarter sales overall grew 5.6%, which doesn’t sound terrible. But organic growth was only 3.1%. The rest came from one-offs like acquisitions and divestitures and foreign exchange benefits.

Drilling down, international sales were up 8% and North American beverage and food sales were roughly flat. This tells you what you need to know about the growth opportunities from here. Expect further strength abroad as the company continues to invest in growth in Latin America, Asia, and Africa. The renovation work at home in North America should continue to boost results there.

North America

Let’s focus on what’s going on in North America, since this is where the biggest opportunity for improvement lies. Growth has slowed down over the past two years, mainly due to sluggish performance as the GLP-1 effect continues to hit sales, and consumers generally turn more health conscious and buy less due to rising costs overall.

The company is taking steps to stem the tide.

It is making products more affordable. In snacks, it is innovating by adding more natural ingredients to make products appear healthier. In beverages, the company is developing in-house brands and looking to brand licensing to expand its presences in non-sparkling categories. It is also investing more in digital marketing.

The tweaks seem to be working. Volumes improved in the third quarter. In food, volume was flat compared to down 2% in the second quarter. Drink sales volume contracted by 2% compared to 4%. Management guides for further improvement. Though like all turnarounds, this one will take time.

[text_ad]

Natural Strengths

PepsiCo has some natural strengths that support both the turnaround effort and the investment thesis.

* Besides the powerful brands, its sheer size ($94 billion in revenue) gives it huge distribution and procurement clout.

PepsiCo ranks number one in the $247 billion global savory snacks market, according to Euromonitor, thanks to well-known brands such as Lay’s, Cheetos, and Doritos. It controls 22% of this space. In drinks, PepsiCo is the world’s second-largest beverage provider behind Coca-Cola (KO), offering popular brands like Gatorade, Pepsi-Cola, and Mountain Dew.

Not surprisingly, the company has close relationships with retailers. Its brands drive foot traffic, making PepsiCo a must-have partner to most retailers. In return, it gets favorable shelf placement.

All of these advantages give PepsiCo a wide moat.

* PepsiCo has defensive characteristics which suggest the stock will hold up if the tech pullback continues, or if we do go into a phase of economic weakness.

* PepsiCo is in excellent financial health. It has a solid balance sheet and strong free cash flow backing a 4.2% dividend yield. It is a net debt/EBITDA ratio of 2.7, which is fairly conservative.

The bottom line: PepsiCo is undervalued, as investors doubt its ability to restore consistent profit growth. Its current price-to-sales ratio of 2 is 21% below the trailing five-year average. The forward price-to-earnings ratio of 16.9 is a 19% discount to the five-year average of 20.9. I suggest betting against the negative investor sentiment, alongside the director who just made a massive stock purchase.

Director Robert Pohlad, with his $23.7 million purchase, is betting these valuation gaps will close as international growth continues and the mini-turnaround continues to bear fruit. He’s worth listening to because he knows the space so well. Pohlad served as chairman and CEO of PepsiAmericas from 2002 until PepsiCo acquired it in 2010. He worked at various PepsiCo distributors for years before 2002. Pohlad, who, along with his family, owns the Minnesota Twins, has been a PepsiCo director since 2015.

data.title: 5 Tech Stocks Hitting 52-Week Highs in the AI Correction
data.description:
The artificial intelligence (AI) boom has hit a wall. After years of impressive gains, investors are starting to question whether the hundreds of billions of dollars being spent on AI infrastructure will generate enough profits to justify the investment.

Those concerns have triggered a sharp selloff in some of the market’s biggest technology stocks.

As of Friday’s close, AI chip giant Nvidia (NVDA) had plunged 24% in the last month, while semiconductor powerhouse Broadcom (AVGO) had fallen 22%. Other AI-related stocks have suffered similar losses over the last one-month period, including Palantir Technologies (PLTR), down 19%, and Meta Platforms (META), down 18%.

The Nasdaq recently entered correction territory, falling more than 10% below its October high while being dragged down by some of the biggest beneficiaries of the AI boom.

But not every technology stock is struggling.

Right now, a grand total of six technology stocks are hitting 52-week highs as the broader technology sector stumbles.

Of note, one of those six technology stocks is STRC, Strategy’s preferred C shares, the Bitcoin-linked preferred stock that appeals to investors for its yield and not its potential for upside momentum.

So, excluding STRC, that leaves us with just five technology stocks that are truly bucking the AI correction. Let’s take a closer look.

[text_ad]

5 Tech Stocks Bucking the AI Selloff

Consensus Cloud Solutions (CCSI)

Consensus Cloud Solutions (CCSI) is one of the most surprising technology winners of 2026. The stock has nearly doubled this year and is currently trading at a 52-week high.

Consensus provides secure digital communications services, including cloud faxing and document delivery. Its products are particularly valuable in healthcare, government and other industries where secure information exchange is essential.

The company’s third-quarter results demonstrated the appeal of predictable recurring revenue. Revenue increased 3.7% to $91 million, while its corporate business grew 9.1%. Adjusted EBITDA reached $47.6 million, representing an impressive 52.3% margin.

Consensus also continues to repurchase shares, buying back approximately 550,000 during the quarter.

The appeal here is straightforward. Investors get a profitable technology company with recurring revenue and strong margins without paying the premium valuations associated with many AI stocks.

Shares have risen 79.5% so far this year and 20.3% over the course of the one-month correction in the Nasdaq.

JFrog (FROG)

JFrog (FROG) is a much more direct beneficiary of the AI revolution.

The company provides software development tools that help businesses manage, secure and distribute their software applications. Its platform helps developers keep track of the software components used in applications and ensure they’re ready for deployment.

That business is becoming increasingly important as AI transforms software development.

AI-powered coding tools can generate enormous amounts of code in a fraction of the time typically demanded of human programmers. But someone still needs to organize, secure and manage all that software.

That’s where JFrog comes in.

The company’s third-quarter results highlight its relevance. Revenue jumped 31% from a year earlier to $179.2 million. Cloud revenue surged 60% to $101.5 million, accounting for 57% of total revenue.

Meanwhile, the number of customers spending more than $1 million annually increased 58% to 112.

Investors liked what they saw. JFrog shares soared more than 35% on November 6 following the earnings announcement, putting the stock back near its record high and pushing the one-year return to 63.2%.

JFrog offers an interesting alternative to the traditional AI trade. Rather than betting on which chipmaker or AI model will ultimately dominate, the company provides tools that businesses need as software development becomes faster and more complex.

But, as with many AI-related names, the biggest concern is valuation, as JFrog is not yet consistently profitable and is trading at an astronomical forward P/E of 90.6.

NIQ Global Intelligence (NIQ)

NIQ Global Intelligence (NIQ), better known as NielsenIQ, is another technology company benefiting from the growing demand for data and analytics.

The company helps retailers and consumer products businesses understand what people are buying, where they’re shopping and how their purchasing habits are changing.

Its enormous collection of consumer data is particularly valuable in the age of artificial intelligence.

AI systems become more useful when they’re trained on reliable, specialized information. NIQ possesses a wealth of proprietary consumer purchasing data that can help businesses make better decisions about pricing, marketing and inventory.

And unlike many emerging AI businesses, NIQ already generates billions of dollars in annual revenue.

Second-quarter revenue increased 8% to $1.12 billion, while adjusted EBITDA climbed nearly 22% to $261.9 million. The company also raised its full-year financial guidance.

Importantly, NIQ is improving profitability and cash generation while continuing to expand its subscription-based intelligence business.

The stock is up 60% in the last year (although it’s worth noting that those returns are on the heels of the company’s post-IPO droop, as it came public in July 2025; the stock is up only 4.1% since the IPO) and recently traded near its highest levels since going public in July 2025.

Block (XYZ)

Block (XYZ), formerly known as Square, is best known for its Cash App digital payments platform and Square payment-processing systems.

But the financial technology company is also becoming increasingly focused on artificial intelligence.

Block is incorporating AI into its products to help merchants manage their operations and consumers make better financial decisions. It also sees opportunities to improve internal efficiency through automation.

More importantly, its underlying businesses are performing well.

Third-quarter gross profit grew 22% to $3.24 billion. Adjusted operating income soared 92% to $923 million, while adjusted earnings per share more than doubled to $1.13.

Cash App gross profit increased 27%, and Square’s gross payment volume grew 14%.

Those strong results prompted management to raise its 2026 financial guidance. The company now expects full-year gross profit of approximately $12.63 billion, representing 22% growth.

Shares have gained more than 30% in the last year and recently reached a new 52-week high (although they’re almost 68% below the all-time highs set in 2021).

Unity Software (U)

Unity Software (U) has been one of the more dramatic turnaround stories in technology.

The company provides software that developers use to create video games and other interactive experiences. It also operates an advertising platform that helps game publishers attract users and generate revenue.

After several difficult years, Unity is showing signs that its turnaround is gaining traction.

Its third-quarter revenue jumped 32% to $622.1 million. More impressively, the company reported its first quarterly GAAP profit since going public.

A major contributor was Unity Vector, its AI-powered advertising technology, which grew 126% year over year.

Vector uses machine learning to improve advertising performance by helping identify the users most likely to engage with an ad or make a purchase, and it’s the reason for the last bout of outperformance.

The stock has gained 20.6% in the last year and just tagged new 52-week highs (although, like Block, shares are well below all-time highs, down 73.5% in the last five years).

The AI Correction Is Creating New Opportunities

The recent technology selloff is primarily hitting the beneficiaries of the AI data center buildout as fears of more stringent regulation, tighter purse strings and overspending weigh on those names.

Investors are ready to move on to the next stage: companies that are actually deploying AI to improve profitability.

Whether that translates to a durable advantage is yet to be seen (and will probably take at least a few quarters of earnings results to suss out).

And there’s no guarantee that these early winners will prove to be long-term winners.

But outperformance in a correction (relative strength) is a powerful trait, and these five tech stocks are the big winners on that front.

data.title: Tread Lightly with Broken AI Stocks
data.description:
Note: For a special video version of Mike’s Cabot Wealth Daily article, “Tread Lightly with Broken AI Stocks,” click here.

“Markets are never wrong; opinions are.”

The above quote came from Jesse Livermore, the infamous trader/plunger/speculator of the early 20th century. To this day, many (including myself) consider Reminiscences of a Stock Operator, a slightly fictionalized biography of Livermore under the name Larry Livingston, the best investing book ever written—highly recommended if you haven’t read it yet.

That said, the above quote came from Livermore’s short book How to Trade in Stocks, which is also a great, quick read and reveals a few tidbits about how he operated back in the day. We had this inscription carved into the mantle of the fireplace in our old office so all of us analysts wouldn’t forget it!

Of course, the quote isn’t to be taken literally: There are obviously times when, say, a stock will tank for months only to reverse higher and recapture lost ground. But the main idea was to avoid arguing with the market—whether amateur or professional—that’s how many investors take on heavy losses, including some of the biggest blowups in history.

I was thinking of this quote recently as we’ve seen the sloppy action in most growth areas turn ugly, especially in tech and AI sectors—frankly, a lot of well-known leaders look intermediate- to longer-term toppy, and some are already slicing through long-term support (40-week moving averages, etc.) and are massively off their highs …

… and yet, at the same time, the firms themselves continue to announce amazing results while often sticking with or raising their multi-year forecasts. Wall Street analysts agree, with growth at most top AI firms expected to remain rapid through 2027, if not much longer. And all that means something has to give: For many fundamentally leading AI names, the valuations are getting very, very tame, especially compared to the expected growth rates.

To be clear, I’m not a valuation guy, but the point is that the market (driven by big investors) is clearly forecasting some sort of AI slowdown or even bust phase starting in the next couple of quarters—while company managements and Wall Street analysts see the historic buildout continuing.

[text_ad]

Take Broadcom (AVGO), one of the leaders in the AI chip space and part of the trillion-dollar market cap club. Growth has obviously been hot (sales up 86%, earnings up 96% in the July quarter), but the top brass says it has a “line of sight” for $230 billion of revenues in fiscal 2028, up from an expected $106 billion this year, with earnings exceeding $30 per share, vs. $11.70 or so seen this year! And yet the stock looks awful, below its 40-week line, no higher than it was 14 months ago and trading at just 17x this coming year’s earnings estimates.

Seagate Technology (STX), one of the two leading plays in hard disk drives, is even more dramatic. In the just-reported September quarter (fiscal Q1 for Seagate), sales (up 61%) and earnings (up 194%) growth remained in the stratosphere, and management said it expects this fiscal year (ending next June) to see meaningfully higher growth than last year; analysts see revenues booming 55%. Meanwhile, the top brass said the vast majority of demand is locked in through calendar 2028 (!), with some deals extended to 2030. But, of course, the stock has tanked, breaking down from a multi-month pattern (nearly 50% off its peak) as it trades at just over 9x earnings estimates for the fiscal year ending next June!

Even lesser-known AI winners are seeing the same pattern. Take TTM Technologies (TTMI), a maker of specialized circuit boards; it does good business in aerospace and defense, but data center demand has kicked growth into overdrive during the past year. And after the recent Q3 report, management remained very bullish, thanks in part to booming orders (more than twice output) and backlog (up more than 100%)--analysts see 2027 bringing sales and earnings growth of nearly 50% and 70%, respectively. But, as with the others, TTMI looks like death, sitting more than 60% off its high, below its 40-week line and trading at less than 10x 2027’s earnings estimates.

My main point in bringing up this topic is simply to highlight the dramatically different viewpoints from the two competing sides—it’s obvious big investors are discounting some sort of mini (or larger) AI slowdown, while analysts and most management teams are saying full speed ahead.

I would expect the tension between the stocks and the numbers to be resolved relatively soon—either some of these names will see big rallies, or analysts are going to have to slash outlooks as reality changes. The most important thing is to remain flexible, but for now anyway, you know my take: In the moment, the market is never wrong, so while bounces are possible/likely, it’s best to tread lightly with these damaged stocks.

[author_ad]

data.title: What the Bond Market Is Telling Us About Leading AI Stocks
data.description:
Most stock traders never look at the credit markets. But right now, the credit market is showing some signs of concern, and everyday investors should be listening, especially as AI stocks have been under selling pressure.

So let’s break down what the credit markets are saying for speculative (CRWV), middle-of-the-road (ORCL) and “safe” (META, GOOG) stocks …

What Is a Credit Default Swap?

A credit default swap (CDS) is insurance on a company’s debt. It’s quoted in basis points (1 bp = 0.01%), so a 100-bp spread costs $100,000 a year to insure $10 million of debt. The higher the number, the more worried the market is. And bond investors tend to spot trouble before stock investors do, which makes CDS one of the best early warning systems an everyday investor can watch.

Options traders will appreciate this: A CDS is essentially a put option on a company’s debt.And since bondholders get paid before stockholders, when credit gets nervous, stocks feel it.

[text_ad]

The Speculative Stock: CoreWeave (CRWV)

CoreWeave’s five-year CDS hit a record on October 15 of about $1 million a year to insure $10 million of its debt. S&P Global Market Intelligence estimates that implies roughly a 64% chance of default over five years. That’s a market-implied number, not a forecast, but the bond market is clearly treating CRWV as a speculative credit, with its 2031 bonds yielding 14% to 16% in mid-October.

And not surprisingly, because of these perceived risks, CRWV stock is trading at a multi-year low.

The Middle Ground: Oracle (ORCL)

Think of a credit rating as a report card for borrowers. Oracle still has a passing grade, what Wall Street calls “investment grade,” but just barely. In July, S&P lowered Oracle to BBB-, the last passing grade before “junk.”

The bond market is even more skeptical. Insuring $10 million of Oracle’s debt now costs about $292,000 a year, more than triple what it cost a year ago. That’s the kind of price usually reserved for junk-rated companies.

Why the worry? Oracle has borrowed heavily to build AI data centers and now owes about $125 billion. And on Monday it said it plans to raise another $20 billion by selling new stock and bonds.

Watch Oracle’s CDS like a thermometer. If it keeps rising and Oracle gets downgraded to junk, many bond funds that can only own investment-grade debt would be forced to sell, and that pressure could spill into the stock.

The “Safe” Stocks: Meta (META) and Alphabet (GOOG)

Even the strongest names in tech are seeing record insurance costs. Insuring $10 million of Meta’s debt cost about $119,000 a year at its late-October peak. For Alphabet, Google’s parent company, that cost has nearly tripled in a year to about $92,000.

But those numbers are a fraction of the more than $1 million it costs to insure the same amount of CoreWeave debt, so it’s not as if traders are racing to buy insurance on the slight chance that Meta and Google are going out of business.

Still, Alphabet just had its worst day ever on October 29, falling 12.6% after reporting that it spent more cash than it brought in last quarter, so it’s possible that traders are getting concerned about the company’s spending now and in the future.

Don’t Trade CDS, But Watch Them

The CDS market is often the canary in the coal mine, and right now that market is getting a bit worried about the spending and future of leading AI companies.

Now you don’t need to trade CDS to use them. Instead, check them like a weather report, and when the forecast turns stormy, make sure you have an exit plan for your stock and options positions.
